problem_statement: A caller needs to reverse the bit order within individual bytes and within byte arrays so that a radio payload can be transmitted and received with the bit ordering required by 802.15.4g (the header uses one bit order while the payload uses the opposite). Today there is no available bit-reversal capability: a request to reverse a single byte, to reverse an array of bytes in place, to reverse an array while copying it to a separate output buffer, and to handle edge cases such as a zero-length array or a single-byte array cannot be performed. Concretely, an observer expects that reversing 0xF0 yields 0x0F, 0xAA yields 0x55, 0x01 yields 0x80, 0x80 yields 0x01, and 0x02 yields 0x40; that reversing a {0xF0,0x0F,0xAA,0x55,0x01,0x80} array in place produces {0x0F,0xF0,0x55,0xAA,0x80,0x01}; that copying {0x01,0x02,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x20,0x40,0x80} into an output buffer yields {0x80,0x40,0x20,0x10,0x08,0x04,0x02,0x01} while leaving the input unchanged; and that a zero-length operation does not crash. The required behavior is that these bit-reversal operations are available and produce the expected reversed results.

superseded_statements.problem_statement: 802.15.4g-compliant radio operation requires the bit order of each byte in the radio payload to be reversed on both transmit and receive, governed by a configuration option; a configuration-controlled payload bit-order mode and the capability it depends on must exist so a radio driver can be built for 802.15.4g and a unit test exercising that capability can be compiled and linked. Currently no such configuration-controlled bit-order capability exists in the codebase, so the capability cannot be enabled and a test that uses it cannot be built.

problem_statement_fixed:
A caller needs to reverse the bit order within individual bytes and within byte arrays so that a radio payload can be transmitted and received with the bit ordering required by 802.15.4g (the header uses one bit order while the payload uses the opposite). Today there is no available bit-reversal capability: a request to reverse a single byte, to reverse an array of bytes in place, to reverse an array while copying it to a separate output buffer, and to handle edge cases such as a zero-length array or a single-byte array cannot be performed. Concretely, an observer expects that reversing 0xF0 yields 0x0F, 0xAA yields 0x55, 0x01 yields 0x80, 0x80 yields 0x01, and 0x02 yields 0x40; that reversing a {0xF0,0x0F,0xAA,0x55,0x01,0x80} array in place produces {0x0F,0xF0,0x55,0xAA,0x80,0x01}; that copying {0x01,0x02,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x20,0x40,0x80} into an output buffer yields {0x80,0x40,0x20,0x10,0x08,0x04,0x02,0x01} while leaving the input unchanged; and that a zero-length operation does not crash. The required behavior is that these bit-reversal operations are available and produce the expected reversed results.

The operations must be exposed as public C functions declared in lib/bitrev.h with the following signatures: uint8_t bitrev_byte(uint8_t byte); void bitrev_array(uint8_t *data, size_t len); void bitrev_array_copy(const uint8_t *input, uint8_t *output, size_t len);. bitrev_byte reverses the bits of a single byte. bitrev_array reverses the bits in each byte of the array pointed to by data in place. bitrev_array_copy copies each bit-reversed byte from input to output and leaves input unchanged. len is the number of bytes to process; a length of 0 means no data is processed and the functions must not crash. A single-byte array is processed like a one-element array, so reversing a one-byte array {0xF0} yields {0x0F}.
